paras: The threatened lynching of Louis Bulling and Peter Hronek took place in St. Joseph, Missouri, in late January and early February 1888, when a mob and then a women's petition sought the lynching of two men held for killing their wives. Police hid Bulling from the mob, no attack on the jail was reported, and both men later went through the courts: Bulling was convicted of second-degree murder and Hronek was hanged legally. The petition, reported as the work of women weary of the law's delay, ran as a wire brief in papers across the country.

Peter Hronek, a Bohemian immigrant of about thirty-two, had shot his wife on April 17, 1887, after accusing her of intimacy with a man living in the same house. By January 1888 he was in the Buchanan County jail under sentence of death. The house where the killing took place belonged to a Mr. Augustine, according to the wire report.

On Sunday afternoon, January 29, 1888, Louis Bulling, twenty-five, went to the Herbert house hotel, where his estranged wife Flora worked as a waiter, locked himself in her room and shot her in the forehead. He was captured by the police, and according to the Omaha Bee's St. Joseph correspondent, "A howling mob was soon on their heels, discovering which the police secreted Bulling." The same dispatch predicted that if he could be found that night he would be "swung to the nearest lamp-post without ceremony."

Bulling was put in the cell held by Hronek, and the St. Paul Globe's correspondent reported "no little excitement and talk of lynching." On February 1 a dispatch from St. Joseph reported that women in one part of the city were circulating a petition to have "Hooneck and Buelling, the wife murderers," lynched, and that it already had several hundred signatures. Mr. Augustine said the women were trying to work up a feeling among "the sterner sex" that would lead the men to take the law into their own hands.

No attempt on the jail appears in the coverage. In April 1888 Louis Buelling was convicted at St. Joseph of murder in the second degree for killing his wife. Hronek was hanged in St. Joseph on June 29, 1888; he denied any intent to kill, and his body was taken to the cathedral of St. Peter and Paul for burial beside his wife.

The story reached readers mainly through a Chicago Times dispatch, which the Washington Evening Star printed on February 2 and the New-York Tribune ran the next day as "Women Demanding Vengeance." Other headlines included "Women Demanding Mob Law" in Wheeling, "Women in Favor of Lynching" in Fort Worth and "Want Them Lynched" in Wilmington. Weeklies from Vermont to South Carolina and West Virginia reprinted the item into mid-February, usually as one or two sentences in a news digest with no comment.

The regional specials gave more color: the Omaha Bee's headline promised "Indignant Citizens Determined to Inflict Summary Punishment," and its correspondent described Bulling as one of the city's most desperate ruffians who had terrorized South St. Joseph. The Missouri paper at Ironton identified the targets by nationality, as "the Bohemian wife-murderer" and "the German wife-murderer."

The wire dispatch placed the petitioners in the southwestern part of the city, while the St. Paul Globe's own correspondent and the Missouri and South Carolina reprints said southeastern. The Globe's February 1 special also named a single target, "Keronk, the Bohemian wife murderer and bully, who killed his wife Sunday night," merging the condemned Bohemian with Bulling, whose killing had taken place that Sunday.
